title: The Timing of Risk Mitigating Strategies
summary: LPL Research examines how different hedging strategies may help manage portfolio risk during short- and long-term periods of market stress.

# The Timing of Risk Mitigating Strategies


[Michael McClain](https://www.lpl.com/research/research-team/michael-mcclain.html) | Alternative Investment Research Analyst and Due Diligence


Last Updated: October 27, 2026


## All Portfolio Hedges Are Not Created Equal


In theory, portfolio hedges share a similar purpose; however, distinctions in design may lead to completely different outcomes, as no single hedge is meant to or able to mitigate against every risk. Some are built to react immediately during a sharp decline, while others require time for a market move to take shape before they contribute, or are designed to work slowly by adding a diversifying return profile across market cycles.


## Building Risk Mitigation Across Time Horizons


Thinking about risk mitigation in terms of time horizons can be more useful than thinking about it in terms of asset classes. The three groups below run on different clocks, and each is designed around a particular type of stress, whether that's a sudden crash, a slow grind lower, or a long stretch when stocks and bonds struggle together, and each may pay off on its own timeline. Viewing them as interchangeable allocations leads to unrealistic expectations and often to abandoning the right hedge at the wrong time (or chasing the performance of a hedge that recently kicked in). Knowing what a hedge is built to do, and when, helps investors size it sensibly and maintain exposure or reduce exposure.


## Week-1 Risk Mitigation


- **Implementation:** Convexity and liquidity for a fast sell-off. This group has two parts. The first is convex hedges, such as puts, long volatility, or dedicated tail-risk programs, with nonlinear payoffs. They pay a premium during calm markets; then they have the potential to gain sharply when volatility jumps, often within days. The second group is safe-haven assets, such as Treasuries and cash. In a growth scare, a flight to quality can lift Treasuries right away. Cash doesn't gain in a crash, but it is available immediately and protects against forced selling.
- **Risk:** Convex hedges need a shock, not just a decline. A slow sell-off may never produce the volatility spike they depend on, and the premium paid while waiting adds up. A hedge can be right about direction and still lose money if cost and timing work against it. Treasuries carry a different risk; they may protect against growth shocks, not inflation shocks. When rising rates are the cause of the sell-off, duration can fall alongside equities.
- **Portfolio Implication:** Depending on how quickly a convex hedge is expected to pay off and to what extent, these allocations may carry a consistent premium that weighs on performance. Pairing them with Treasuries and cash may offset the cost of the hedge and add a source of risk mitigation during a flight to safety.


## Month-1 Risk Mitigation


- **Implementation:** As managed futures strategies may invest long and short across equity, bond, commodity, and currency markets, during an extended sell-off, their price-based signals may reposition portfolios to capitalize on how markets often move during a drawdown (short equity, long bonds, long gold, long safe haven currencies). As a trend usually requires several weeks to form before they can position for it, during the initial part of a sell-off, these strategies may still be leaning the wrong way. However, once a drawdown persists, they may gain in several markets at once, and the benefit tends to build the longer the decline lasts.
- **Risk:** As trend strategies take time to react, a sharp V-shaped rebound may catch them on the wrong side of a change in the existing trend direction, and profits from a sell-off can fade once the market changes direction.
- **Portfolio Implication:** Managed futures are one of the few hedges that can work when stocks and bonds fall together, which fills the gap left by Treasuries in an inflation shock. However, if a strategy is positioned with long equity exposure at the start of a sell-off, they may experience losses until the drawdown is strong enough for their models to go short.


## Full-Cycle Risk Mitigation


- **Implementation:** Diversifying strategies that may perform well across market cycles. Global macro, equity market neutral, and multi-strategy strategies.
- **Risk:** Manager selection, macro risks, and factor crashes that have a negative impact across asset classes.
- **Portfolio Implications:** These strategies reduce reliance on the stock-bond relationship, help fund the carrying costs of convex hedges, and provide capital to rebalance at lows. Over a full cycle, these allocations are expected to have limited beta and correlation to traditional equity and bond markets, with a volatility profile roughly half that of the equity market.

## Three Drawdowns, Three Different Winners


- **2020:** Fast crash scenario, as the S&P 500 lost roughly a third of its value in under a month. This was Week-1 Risk Mitigation territory, as long volatility strategies ranked at or near the top of hedge fund performance in the first quarter.
- **2022:** A slow grind, as inflation and an aggressive Federal Reserve drove a drawdown that unfolded over months. For the year, the S&P 500 fell 18.1% and the Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate lost 13.0%. As the drawdown developed over the year, Week-1 risk mitigators could not provide the same type of ballast as they do during a fast crash. However, managed futures profited from short equity and bond exposure as both markets moved lower.
- **2008:** A longer drawdown cycle, as the Global Financial Crisis featured a grinding decline followed by a sharp panic. Investors holding all three types of risk mitigating strategies were supported, as addition to the Week-1 and Month-1 support, global macro and market neutral strategies protected during the sell-offs, while also adding value through security selection during the dislocation.


## LPL Research Takeaway


No single hedge is consistently better than the others, rather each is suited to a different type of drawdown, and no one can know in advance which kind is coming. The cost of put protection during 2022, or a trend allocation caught off guard in February 2020, looks like a mistake on its own. However, as part of a complete risk mitigation sleeve, each was waiting for the drawdown it was built for. We believe the most durable approach combines risk mitigation across all three time frames and sizes of each piece to what the portfolio can afford to hold. Before asking whether a hedge worked, advisors and clients may be better served by asking what kind of drawdown it was built for, and whether that drawdown has arrived.


*Additional disclosures: Managed futures are speculative, use significant leverage, may carry substantial charges, and should only be considered suitable for the risk capital portion of an investor's portfolio. A tail risk program is a dedicated strategy, usually run by a specialist manager, built to make money in rare, severe market crashes (the "left tail" of the return distribution). It mostly holds out-of-the-money put options and other volatility instruments. In normal markets it costs a small, steady amount, and in a sharp sell-off it can pay out many times that cost.*
